Breed means to cause something new to come into existence from something that already exists — whether that "something new" is a living baby animal, a type of creature, a feeling, or a situation.

Think of breed as a "production" word — one thing acting as a source that produces another thing out of itself. Keep this image in your mind and every meaning of the word will make sense.
Meaning 1: Animals Naturally Producing Offspring

When animals mate and produce young, they breed.

  • Rabbits breed very fast.
  • These birds breed in spring.
  • Sharks breed slowly, which makes them vulnerable to extinction.

Here, the animal itself is the subject. No human is involved. It simply means the natural act of reproducing — one generation giving rise to the next.
Meaning 2: Humans Controlling Animal Reproduction

When a person deliberately selects which animals mate with each other — so that the offspring grow up to have specific, desirable qualities — that person is breeding those animals.

  • Farmers breed cows to produce more milk.
  • She breeds racehorses for speed and endurance.
  • Scientists breed fruit flies in the lab to study genetics.

Notice the key difference from Meaning 1: in Meaning 1, the animal does it on its own. In Meaning 2, a human is in charge, steering the process with a goal in mind. The human wants the offspring to be bigger, stronger, calmer, more beautiful — and so chooses the parents carefully. This is often called selective breeding.
Meaning 3: One Condition Producing Another (Figurative — Very Common)

This is one of the most widely used senses of breed in everyday English, and you will encounter it constantly. Here, breed means to cause something — usually a feeling, quality, or situation — to develop and grow as a result of something else.

Just as a mother animal produces offspring, a circumstance or situation can "give birth to" a certain outcome — and English uses breed for that.

  • "Poverty breeds crime." → Poverty causes crime to grow and spread.
  • "Fear breeds hatred." → Fear gives rise to hatred.
  • "Success breeds confidence." → Success naturally produces more confidence.
  • "Boredom breeds trouble." → Having nothing to do leads to trouble.

The pattern is always: [Cause] breeds [Effect].

The cause acts like a parent; the effect is what it produces. This figurative use is very powerful in English because it suggests that the effect doesn't appear by accident — it grows naturally and inevitably out of the cause, the same way an offspring grows from its parent.
Meaning 4: A Place or Environment Producing Something

Closely related to Meaning 3, but here the focus is on a physical place or condition that acts as the source — like a hotbed from which something grows.

  • "Stagnant water breeds mosquitoes." → Still, dirty water is the environment where mosquitoes grow and multiply.
  • "Dark, damp walls breed mold." → Those conditions cause mold to develop and thrive.
  • "The city bred a new kind of music." → The city was the fertile ground where a new musical style grew and came alive.

Here, the place or condition is almost acting like a parent — it nurtures and produces what grows within it. In fact, the term breeding ground comes directly from this idea: a breeding ground is any place (physical or figurative) where something undesirable grows easily.

  • "That neighborhood became a breeding ground for gang activity."
  • "Overcrowded prisons are breeding grounds for radicalization."
Meaning 5: Raising and Shaping a Person

In a more formal or old-fashioned sense, breed can mean to raise a child in a particular environment, with particular values, so that they grow up to be a certain kind of person. You will most often see this in the passive form: was bred / were bred.

  • "She was bred to lead." → From childhood, her upbringing and training shaped her to be a leader.
  • "He was bred for discipline and loyalty." → His entire upbringing instilled discipline and loyalty in him.
  • "They were bred in luxury." → They grew up in a wealthy, privileged environment.

The logic is the same as selective animal breeding — just applied to humans. The environment, the family, and the upbringing are "selecting" what the person becomes.
The Thread That Connects All Meanings

No matter which meaning you encounter, breed always carries this core idea:

Something already in existence acts as a source, and something new comes out of it.

  • A rabbit breeds → new rabbits come out.
  • A farmer breeds cattle → a better type of cattle comes out.
  • Poverty breeds crime → crime grows out of poverty.
  • Stagnant water breeds mosquitoes → mosquitoes multiply out of that environment.
  • An upbringing breeds a certain character → a person's qualities come out of how they were raised.

The "output" always emerges from, and is shaped by, the "input." That relationship is the soul of the word.
Active vs. Passive: "Breed" and "Be Bred"

You will frequently see breed in the passive voice, especially for Meanings 4 and 5:

  • "Contempt is bred by overfamiliarity." → Overfamiliarity produces contempt.
  • "Good manners are bred at home." → A good home produces good manners.
  • "He was bred for war." → His entire upbringing prepared him for war.

In the active form, the focus is on the cause doing the producing. In the passive form, the focus shifts to what is being produced.
Important Expressions That Use "Breed"

"Familiarity breeds contempt"
The more familiar you are with something or someone, the more you begin to take it for granted or lose respect for it. Knowing someone too well removes the sense of awe or care you once had for them. This is one of the most famous English proverbs that uses breed.

"Born and bred"
Used to say that someone was both born in a place and grew up there — and that the place deeply shaped who they are.

  • "He's Manchester born and bred." → He was born in Manchester and grew up there; the city made him who he is.

"Breeding ground"
A place or situation where something (often something bad) grows and spreads easily.

  • "The prison became a breeding ground for extremist ideas."
A Quick Summary

UseWhat BreedsWhat It Produces

In plain words:

  • Animals producing offspring → natural reproduction.
  • Humans guiding animal reproduction → producing desired traits on purpose.
  • A condition producing an outcome → one thing inevitably giving rise to another.
  • A place producing something → an environment nurturing what grows in it.
  • An upbringing producing a person's character → shaping who someone becomes.

Every single use of breed is a variation of one idea: a source producing an outcome from within itself. Once you hold onto that image, you will instinctively understand breed in any sentence you ever encounter it.
